newsitem.title: UK: Guinness sees pain from sterling strength.
newsitem.headline: Guinness sees pain from sterling strength.

text.p: Drinks group Guinness Plc said on Wednesday the strong pound would cut profits by six percent or 60 million pounds in 1997 compared to 1996 assuming current exchange rates hold.
It also said sales by its spirits arm United Distillers' were one percent higher than in 1995 with notable growth in single malts and de luxe Scotch whiskies.
Total Scotch sales have recovered well in the second half, said the company.
Most country markets have traded in line with the group's forecasts, with trading in Latin America improving in the second half as Venezuela and Mexico recovering annual profits.
"Business continues to be strong in Asia, with further progress in many markets, notably in Thailand, South East Asia and Korea," said the group.
But it said "unfavourable economic conditions continue to constrain sales in Europe." In Britain shelf prices of leading brands were kept at "target levels" over the Christmas period.
Premium imported brands in the U.S. have done well with depletions running ahead of shipments and growth in the emerging markets of Eastern Europe has continued to be strong, Guinness said.

United Distillers has achieved price increases of three percent or more during 1996 in the U.S., Britain, Latin America, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. The effect of these price increases will be around 1.5 percent for 1996.
Guinness stout has increased volumes sold by five percent and draught Guinness by eight percent in 1996.
But the company said the beer market in Spain has remained difficult, declining four percent. Drinkers switched from high margin on premise beer to lower margin take home.
But Cruzcampo profits for 1996 are expected to be broadly in line with 1995 due to improved productivity.
Although the strength of sterling is likely to affect the company, this will be partly offset by a lower interest charge on their debt.
It said its interest charge would be "somewhat lower than current market expectations for 1997, reducing the interest coupon by over 1 full precentage point compared to 1996."
Analysts estimate this represents a saving of 10-15 million pounds.
